It looks good but unless you're going to do ***something*** with it, then it's just a "vibe". To me, *slop* is a *vibe* that someone thinks is "ready for production" and they genuinely have no clue what it means to be ready for production. 

But in all honesty, I really want to see the "built a game in one day" posts or "built a game in one prompt" go away yesterday. It's genuinely not very helpful and just something that everyone is trying to do and have seen tons of posts about. 

"A game" should be complete with actual things to do and accomplish. Let's see multiple levels, with a story, several bosses and mini bosses, what's your progression system like, theres a lot more to it than just asking ai to "build a game and make no mistakes"... Not just a sandbox/prototype.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
What is the game’s objective? What is the core loop? What puts pressure on the player to advance?

Where could you add more game feel? Where is the transition between water and not? Are there day/night cycles. What visual tells are there on potential interactions?

There are dozens of questions to be answered at every single moment of game development. If you are actively seeking out and answering these questions then it is not slop. The longer you do that for the less sloppy your game becomes. Instead it becomes polished.

replies.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
replies.body:
I think these questions aren't relevant to a prototype.

That's my take. Usually, you write a prototype to either get a feel for a game loop or to try to develop or flesh out some mechanic.

One example I've seen a video on was [Braid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braid_(video_game)).  They walked through how the game was developed and it basically was "Mario Bros but you have control of time!". The dev's first goal with a prototype was to see if they could make the "time mechanic" work. Being able to rewind any given moment in the game.

It was very basic. More basic that what we see here from OP. It was barely anything. A single box screen and just trying to get the mechanic to work.

Usually, that's the goal of a prototype. You're either fleshing out a specific new mechanic to see how it "feels" and maybe tune it to see if it's fun or a game loop in a tight context.

This prototype... doesn't feel like it has an explicit goal...

I couldn't find the Braid video but I found another... it starts VERY basic because they're trying to feel out the game's loop..

Here's a video for another game:  [Thronefall](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2239150/Thronefall/)

For Thronefall, they start with how it looks... and that's super key because you want your product to be identifiable and this is the BIGGEST challenge of  AI... Art from generative AI, is by definition, already created. There is nothing new or creative... and so most AI games, have a very "samey" feel because the image is a result of already created images being brought together to find, basically, the "mean" of the visual. (that's a simplified explanation but gets the point across)

Then they still do research on how the game feels and the core loop while also STILL experimenting with the visuals.

That's the purpose of a prototype to, see if an idea is viable... the problem with AI Games, is it's too good at making anything "feel" viable... and in truth it's just boring or not interesting...

Forget objective... OP is making a Tropical Survival game and those, already exist in abundance and they offer nothing new... if they plan on making a game to sell or for other people to play... they're going to need to offer something more than what we see mechanically.

replies.author: xepherys
replies.body:
I agree, but this would be "slop" even without AI. If OP coded it by hand as an entry level project, it would get a "good job - now what?" but it still wouldn't be a showstopper. But given that it was done via AI and has no real interest, benefit, or use, it is de facto slop. 

The same thing was true when Unity first became popular years and years ago and the Steam Store was suddenly full of shit games. Back then we called it "shovelware". It was still just slop, even without AI. The "AI slop" term is used way too often to be useful, but the sentiment predates AI and is still relevant.

comments.author: xepherys
comments.body:
It would be "slop" even if you didn't use AI. What's it's purpose? People seem to not understand that just because AI can help you code a game (or code one for you), the design element is still necessary. It's that lack of design that makes it slop, whether it's "AI slop" or "human slop". 

What's the intent? Is it supposed to be a tech demo for some mechanic that your video doesn't provide? Or is it literally "look I'm on a jetski with a pew omgsocool"? Because it looks like the latter. And if that's all it was and you hand-coded it, the only difference might be that you're showing you got something like this working, by hand, with your own brain and time. That would, at least, take it from "slop" to "good job - now what are you going to do with it?" which is still the question anyway.

replies.author: Potential-Edge5326
replies.body:
I think we just disagree on what “slop” means. If “slop” is simply “something that doesn’t have enough design depth or a sufficiently serious purpose,” then the term becomes so broad that you could apply it to tons of things.   
  
And in my case, there really isn’t some grand intent behind it. I was messing around, made a jetski and a gun because I thought it was fun, and shared it. I’m not presenting it as the next great game design achievement. Sometimes making a silly thing because it’s entertaining is enough. It’s really not that deep.

replies.author: xepherys
replies.body:
But that *is* the definition of slop. Prior to AI, "slop" was still a term used for pretty much the same purpose, which is why these days we mostly hear about "AI slop" specifically. Slop has always existed. Years ago it was "shovelware" or "Unity slop" that flooded the Steam Store. The term "slop" was used 150 years ago regarding pulp fiction mills that just spit out slop upon slop to the eager consumer. "Slop" was used to describe a lot of early mass-produced items, and in the last 20 years or so, "Chinese slop" was specifically used to describe low-quality mass produced garbage - basically what we mostly see on Temu still today. 

So yes, it *is* a broad term, and yes it *can* be applied to tons of things and always has been. I'm not trying to be a dick here, but I'm guessing that you're Gen Z or younger. It's odd to me that so many people under 25-28 or so seem to think that nothing existed prior to the time they were kids. I've experienced it with my own Gen Z kids and it's wild - like you were all born with all of human knowledge in your pockets and somehow know less about general knowledge than most people even a few years older.

I'm not trying to take away your sense of accomplishment. Creating *anything* is cool, even if it's completely done by AI through your guidance. I use AI *a lot* these days for a lot of different things. But I also accept that I sometimes make slop as well. Hell, I've written slop code before AI was anything other than distant science fiction. I've occasionally written slop for 40+ years, and doing it by hand didn't make it any less "slop".
